requirements.requirement: The diagram makes clear how admission, routing, caching, fallback, streaming, capacity protection, and accounting interact, especially under overload and provider failure.
requirements.brief_evidence: “The diagram should make clear how admission, routing, caching, fallback, streaming, capacity protection, and accounting interact, especially how requests behave under overload and provider failure.”

representation_evidence.observation: The normal admission-to-queue-to-cache-to-policy-to-router-to-attempt-to-stream-to-metering path is visible, with breaker feedback and retry sections. However, overload admission limits, provider-failure classes, non-retryable return, retry invariants, and post-stream failure behavior are not clear.

Major clusters and several interactions are connected, but spend protection and shadow evaluation are disconnected, and multiple required failure/overload transitions have no structured representation.

requirements.note: Normal-flow interaction is strong, while the requested overload and provider-failure operational contract is substantially incomplete.

verdict.strongest_covered_cluster: The normal request path is strongest: one capability-tier endpoint, authentication and tenant/quota resolution, deadline-aware queuing, exact/semantic cache, prompt context and safety policy, tier-aware routing using health/latency/depth/price/residency, hosted and self-hosted capacity, streaming, and billing/audit destinations.
verdict.most_consequential_gap: Failure and overload semantics are incomplete: admission omits concurrency and token-rate limits, retries omit fresh deadlines and idempotency, non-retryable return is absent, and the no-cross-backend-retry rule after streaming starts is absent.
verdict.coverage_summary: The board represents the main architecture and normal routing path well, including capacity choices, cache, prompt policy, breaker/probe concepts, accounting, and shadow-result isolation. Weighted coverage is 43/71 = 0.6056. Several system-defining admission and failure-contract requirements are absent, while many others retain only their component label without the required qualifier or outcome. The board therefore cannot replace the brief as a visual acceptance record.
